sketches.title: Bureaucracy Breaks: Officials Stunned by Ordinary Form
sketches.premise: The House announces a boring, checkable fact as if it has shattered civilization. You and the House get the same fact and write competing tabloid headlines; the Judge awards points for how dramatically you escalate without changing what the fact actually says.
sketches.criterion: The headline must keep the fact’s subject, action, and outcome true while making its shock, stakes, and attitude increasingly ridiculous.
sketches.move_shape: Write one headline of no more than 160 characters, using the fact’s two nouns and keeping its factual relationship intact; example for “library / chair”: “LIBRARY CHAIR SURVIVES ANOTHER DAY—EXPERTS CALL IT A MIRACLE OF FURNITURE.”

sketches.title: Tiny Truth Scandal: Nation Outraged by a Completely Normal Detail
sketches.premise: A dull fact enters the courtroom, and both players turn it into a scandalous tabloid headline. The Judge checks whether the headline still reports the fact, then rewards the biggest leap in outrage, innuendo, or accusation that does not smuggle in a new event.
sketches.criterion: The headline must preserve the fact exactly while changing only its framing, implication, and emotional temperature.
sketches.move_shape: Write a one-line headline that names both supplied nouns and preserves their real connection; example for “bus / stop”: “BUS STOPS AT BUS STOP—COMMUTERS DEMAND ANSWERS, SNACKS, AND PERHAPS A REFUND.”
sketches.first_card: A bus stops at a bus stop.

sketches.title: Ordinary Object Witness: The Evidence Is Tragically Mundane
sketches.premise: The House and you receive the same two-noun fact and publish rival headlines about it. Then each player calls which headline better hides the real fact inside a lurid performance; the card’s truth is read aloud after the calls.
sketches.criterion: The headline must retain the card’s checkable fact and both nouns, while its added claims remain clearly framing rather than replacements for that fact.
sketches.move_shape: Write a headline no longer than 160 characters; example for “soap / sink”: “SOAP FOUND IN SINK—BATHROOM AUTHORITIES CONFIRM THE SUSPECT IS, AT LEAST, CLEAN.”

sketches.title: The Normality Files: Investigators Confirm Nothing Happened
sketches.premise: Each round, a plain fact is treated as a classified revelation. Both players write a headline that makes the ordinary sound dangerous, romantic, or politically explosive, and the Judge scores the stretch that still leaves the fact recognizable and true.
sketches.criterion: The headline must keep the supplied nouns and their real-world relationship true, even while its tone implies a much larger story.
sketches.move_shape: Write one tabloid headline, using both nouns, that adds attitude without adding a contradictory fact; example for “dog / bowl”: “DOG APPROACHES BOWL AGAIN—FAMILY FEARS THE ANIMAL MAY HAVE A PLAN.”
sketches.first_card: A dog eats from a bowl.

sketches.title: Headline Under Oath: No Lies, Maximum Drama
sketches.premise: You are a reporter with one sacred rule: the boring fact cannot be false. The House writes its own headline from the same card, then the Judge awards points for the funniest, sharpest, most outrageous presentation that survives cross-examination.
sketches.criterion: The headline must state or unmistakably preserve the card’s complete checkable truth, with invented motives and consequences allowed only as obvious commentary rather than altered facts.
sketches.move_shape: Write a single headline using the card’s two nouns; example for “rain / window”: “RAIN HITS WINDOW—GLASS REFUSES TO COMMENT AS WEATHER RETURNS TO ITS OLD TRICKS.”

sketches.title: Shrugworthy Shockwave: Experts Horrified by the Expected
sketches.premise: The House and you compete to turn a fact worthy of a shrug into front-page chaos. Your headline earns more points the farther it travels into roast, menace, romance, or profanity while the original fact remains safely alive underneath.
sketches.criterion: The headline must keep the card’s two-noun fact true and identifiable, while everything else may be invented, exaggerated, or gloriously tasteless.
sketches.move_shape: Write one headline of up to 160 characters containing both nouns; example for “shoe / floor”: “SHOE DISCOVERED ON FLOOR—ROOMMATE LAUNCHES INVESTIGATION, THEN SITS DOWN AND DOES FUCK-ALL.”
sketches.first_card: A shoe is on the floor.
